original_value: All human communication involves the use of signs. By following a mutually shared set of signs and rules, meaning can be conveyed from one entity to another. Cartographic semiology provides such a theoretical framework, suggesting how to apply visual variables with respect to thematic content. However, semiotics does not address how the choice and composition of such visual variables may lead to different connotations, interpretations, or judgments. The research herein aimed to identify perceived similarities between geometric shape symbols as well as strategies and processes underlying these similarity judgments. Based on a user study with 38 participants, the (dis)similarities of a set of 12 basic geometric shapes (e.g., circle, triangle, square) were examined. Findings from cluster analysis revealed a three-cluster configuration, while multidimensional scaling further quantified the proximities between the geometric shapes in a two-dimensional space. Qualitative and quantitative content analyses identified four strategies underlying the participants’ similarity judgments, namely visual, affective, associative, and behavioral strategies. With the findings combined, this research provides a differentiated perspective on shape proximities, cognitive relations, and the processes involved.

result.paraphrase: Human communication relies on signs; when people share the same system of signs and rules, meaning can be transferred between entities. Cartographic semiology offers a theoretical framework for assigning visual variables in relation to thematic content. Semiotics, however, does not explain how the selection and arrangement of these visual variables can produce different connotations, interpretations, or judgments. This study sought to determine perceived similarities among geometric shape symbols and to uncover the strategies and processes behind those similarity judgments. Using a user study with 38 participants, it examined the (dis)similarities of 12 basic geometric shapes, such as circles, triangles, and squares. Cluster analysis indicated a three-cluster structure, and multidimensional scaling measured the shapes’ closeness in two-dimensional space. Qualitative and quantitative content analysis identified four strategies driving participants’ similarity judgments: visual, affective, associative, and behavioral. Taken together, the results offer a nuanced view of shape proximity, cognitive relations, and the processes involved.
